abstract: Pathological transitions in nervous tissue, including epileptiform discharges and cortical spreading depolarization, depend on the interplay between cellular and interstitial mechanisms. We develop a biophysically detailed two-dimensional model of the neurogliovascular unit (NGVU) integrating neuronal populations in the Hodgkin-Huxley formalism, astrocyte-regulated extracellular potassium dynamics, extracellular neurotransmitter spillover, and noradrenergic neuromodulation. Numerical simulations show that inhibitory interneurons enter depolarization block (DB) at significantly lower extracellular potassium concentrations and stimulation intensities than pyramidal neurons. Early loss of inhibition shifts the local excitation-inhibition balance and triggers network hyperexcitability. In the spatially extended network, exceeding a critical stimulation threshold induces a transition from heterogeneous but spatially uniform firing to network fragmentation into stable active microclusters with self-sustained high-frequency firing. Pyramidal neurons with lower excitatory synaptic input receive less recurrent excitation, which protects them from DB. By continuously releasing potassium ions and glutamate into the extracellular space, pyramidal neurons drive strong depolarization in more densely connected neighbors and push them into deep DB. Simulations of localized astrocytic dysfunction predict a spatial limit for potassium clearance defects. Small damaged cores are fully compensated by diffusion and uptake by surrounding healthy astrocyte units. However, above a critical damage size, activity-dependent potassium buildup and firing positive feedback disrupt homeostasis in surrounding units, promoting persistent depolarized centers with self-sustained, spatially segregated pathological activity.
